metadata.system_name: Event framework with tightly inter-dependent application logic and framework

evaluation_inputs.system_description: An Event framework where the application logic and framework are highly inter-dependent. The Main module is part of the framework, and the Event Manager interacts directly with application handlers. It features an Event Queue and a base Handler component extended by standard and application-specific handlers.

phase_1_discovery.initial_documentation_status: Fully developed architecture with class diagrams, component descriptions, and defined component interactions.
evaluator_inquiry_questions: Can the components of the architecture be reused for future projects?
Can the framework be expanded in the future to accommodate a new application or new components?
Will the system handle any input given by the user and handle invalid input?
Is the architecture consistent in behavior?
Can any new application-specific functionality be added to the architecture?
Can the system be modified in short time and cost-effective manner?
Does the architecture perform its event-processing task properly?

hardware_view_description: System accepts input via Command Line Interface (CLI)
Single processor execution implied (sequential event processing)
runtime_constraints: Events must be dispatched in a First-Come-First-Served (FIFO) pattern
System must maintain an 'idle wait' state until input is received
Application logic is embedded within framework components

quantitative_model_parameters.performance_proxy: Number of components involved in a transaction
quantitative_model_parameters.transaction_speed: Qualitative (Slow due to high number of components involved)

questions: Does the system allow unauthorized access?
Does the architecture portray data confidentiality?
Does the architecture process any task in the fastest possible speed?

architectural_approaches.approach_name: Tightly coupled event framework with embedded application logic
architectural_approaches.description: The supplied system description states that application logic and framework are highly inter-dependent, and that application logic is embedded within framework components. The Main module is part of the framework, and the Event Manager interacts directly with application handlers.

addressed_attributes.rationale: Direct interaction between the Event Manager and application handlers supports event dispatch and handler execution.
A single framework-centered design can keep behavior within one structure, though the supplied evidence also indicates tight coupling.
Sequential processing with a single processor and one event queue aligns with the implied FIFO event flow, but no speed improvement is evidenced.

architectural_approaches.approach_name: Single event queue with FIFO dispatch and idle-wait execution
architectural_approaches.description: The architecture context explicitly identifies one Event Queue, FIFO dispatch, and idle-wait until input is received, with sequential execution on a single processor.

addressed_attributes.rationale: The queue and idle-wait behavior support accepting input, buffering it, and processing events in order.
FIFO dispatch provides predictable ordering, and idle-wait behavior reflects controlled readiness for input.
The quantitative model notes one queue and sequential processing, but also states transaction speed is qualitatively slow due to the number of components involved.

architectural_approaches.approach_name: Base handler extended by standard and application-specific handlers
architectural_approaches.description: The system includes a base Handler component that is extended by standard and application-specific handlers, indicating inheritance-based variability for event handling.

addressed_attributes.rationale: Extension via specialized handlers supports adding new behavior through new subclasses rather than changing the base handler contract, based on the supplied description.
A shared base Handler component can be reused by standard and application-specific handler variants.
The existence of standard and application-specific handler extensions indicates support for variation points in event handling.

architectural_approaches.approach_name: Fixed framework limits for manager and queue count
architectural_approaches.description: The quantitative model specifies architecture limits of one Event Manager and one Event Queue.

addressed_attributes.rationale: A constrained set of central components can simplify the architectural model.
The limit constrains concurrency and may contribute to the stated slow transaction speed, though no improvement evidence is provided.
Fixed component counts may constrain later scaling or reconfiguration; this is an inferred risk from the supplied limits.

scenario_reference.text: No unauthorized access to the system

analysis_records.environment: CLI-based operation with events arriving to the framework
analysis_records.stimulus: An unauthorized user attempts to access or invoke the system
analysis_records.response_measure: Access is denied; no unauthorized event execution occurs
architectural_decisions: The supplied architecture evidence describes event handling, queueing, and handler extension, but does not mention authentication or authorization mechanisms.
Application logic is embedded within framework components, increasing coupling between framework access and application behavior.
analysis_records.reasoning: Because the evidence does not describe security controls, no conclusion can be made that unauthorized access is prevented. The architecture may handle events correctly, but that does not imply access control. The coupling between framework and application logic also does not itself provide security.

risks.description: No explicit authorization mechanism is evidenced for event access
risks.rationale: The supplied inputs mention CLI input, FIFO dispatch, and handlers, but no authentication or authorization control. The security scenario therefore remains unverified and potentially at risk.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Presence or absence of authentication/authorization checks before dispatch

scenario_reference.text: All operations are processed in fastest possible speed

analysis_records.environment: Single-processor, sequential event processing under normal input load
analysis_records.stimulus: A user submits operations through the CLI for execution
analysis_records.response_measure: Transaction latency is minimized; operations complete at the fastest achievable rate
architectural_decisions: The architecture uses one Event Manager and one Event Queue.
Sequential FIFO event dispatch is required.
The performance proxy is the number of components involved in a transaction, and the supplied qualitative assessment says transactions are slow due to the number of components involved.
analysis_records.reasoning: The evidence directly suggests slower performance, not fastest possible speed. A single queue and sequential dispatch can preserve order, but they do not indicate high throughput. The proxy also increases with component count, which is explicitly characterized as slow.

risks.description: Sequential multi-component event processing is likely to limit speed
risks.rationale: The system is constrained to one Event Manager, one Event Queue, and FIFO sequential execution, and the supplied proxy labels the resulting transaction speed as slow due to the number of components involved.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Number of components involved in a transaction

scenario_reference.text: Any failure should be followed by immediate recovery

analysis_records.stimulus: A handler, queue operation, or dispatch step fails
analysis_records.response_measure: The system recovers immediately and continues event processing
architectural_decisions: The architecture includes an Event Queue, Event Manager, and base Handler hierarchy.
The provided evidence does not describe recovery, retry, rollback, or fault isolation mechanisms.
analysis_records.reasoning: Without explicit recovery mechanisms, immediate recovery cannot be substantiated. The architecture structure supports event processing, but the evidence does not show how failures are contained or recovered from.

risks.description: Recovery behavior after failure is unspecified
risks.rationale: The architecture description does not provide any failure handling or recovery design, so immediate recovery remains unsupported.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Presence of retry/recovery/error-isolation logic in handlers or manager

scenario_reference.text: User errors in using system should be handled

analysis_records.stimulus: A user enters invalid or malformed input
analysis_records.response_measure: The system detects invalid input and handles it without crashing
architectural_decisions: The system accepts input via CLI and maintains an idle wait state until input is received.
The evidence does not describe validation logic, error messages, or exception handling for invalid input.
analysis_records.reasoning: The CLI entry point makes input validation relevant, but no evidence shows that invalid input is handled. The idle-wait behavior concerns readiness, not error tolerance.

risks.description: Invalid CLI input handling is not evidenced
risks.rationale: The available architecture evidence describes how input is received but not how malformed or erroneous input is validated or rejected.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Validation and error-handling logic at the CLI boundary

scenario_reference.text: New demands on system functionality should be accommodated

analysis_records.environment: Future extension request after initial deployment
analysis_records.stimulus: A new functional requirement must be added
analysis_records.response_measure: The change is implemented with limited impact to existing framework components
architectural_decisions: The base Handler is extended by standard and application-specific handlers.
Application logic is embedded within framework components.
The framework has a single Event Manager and a single Event Queue.
The architecture is described as highly inter-dependent between application logic and framework.
analysis_records.reasoning: Handler extension suggests some ability to add new functionality, but tight coupling and embedded logic can make changes broader and more invasive. The evidence supports growth potential but not low-cost change.

risks.description: High coupling may make new functionality invasive to add
risks.rationale: Application logic is embedded in framework components and the architecture is highly inter-dependent, which can increase the scope of change for new demands.

non_risks.description: Handler inheritance provides a visible extension mechanism
non_risks.rationale: The base Handler is extended by standard and application-specific handlers, which suggests some support for adding functionality through extension rather than wholesale replacement.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Degree of coupling between framework and application logic

scenario_reference.text: Major parts of the framework should be re-usable for future architectures

analysis_records.stimulus: A different project wants to reuse major framework parts
analysis_records.response_measure: Major framework parts can be reused with limited rework
architectural_decisions: The architecture is highly inter-dependent between application logic and framework.
The Main module is part of the framework.
Handlers are extended from a common base component.
analysis_records.reasoning: Common base handlers may support reuse of some behavior, but embedding application logic in framework components and coupling Main to the framework reduce portability of major parts to unrelated architectures. Reuse is therefore uncertain and potentially limited.

risks.description: Strong interdependence may limit reuse of major framework parts
risks.rationale: The architecture explicitly states that application logic and framework are highly inter-dependent, which can hinder extraction and reuse in future architectures.

non_risks.description: Shared base handler structure may enable partial reuse
non_risks.rationale: A base Handler extended by standard and application-specific handlers indicates some reusable abstraction exists.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Extent to which application logic remains embedded in framework components

scenario_reference.text: Components in framework interact in a coordinated manner

analysis_records.stimulus: Framework components exchange control during event processing
analysis_records.response_measure: Components interact according to the documented interaction model
architectural_decisions: The Event Manager interacts directly with application handlers.
The framework includes an Event Queue and a base Handler component.
Component interactions are described as defined in the architecture documentation.
analysis_records.reasoning: The architecture provides defined interactions and a single event-processing path, which supports coordinated behavior. However, the direct interaction with application handlers also implies coupling that could complicate evolution.

non_risks.description: Defined component interactions support coordinated behavior
non_risks.rationale: The documentation states that component interactions are defined and that the Event Manager interacts directly with handlers, supporting consistent orchestration.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Clarity and stability of component interaction contracts

tradeoff_points.parameter: Direct interaction between Event Manager and handlers

scenario_reference.text: Framework expansion is possible to allow for more sophisticated options

analysis_records.stimulus: A need arises to add more sophisticated framework options
analysis_records.response_measure: Expansion is feasible without major redesign
architectural_decisions: The architecture contains a base Handler that is extended by specialized handlers.
The system has a single Event Manager and single Event Queue.
The framework and application logic are highly inter-dependent.
analysis_records.reasoning: The base handler hierarchy suggests extension points, but the tight coupling and single-manager/single-queue structure may make broader expansion harder. Evidence supports some extension capability, but not seamless expansion.

risks.description: Tight coupling may constrain broader expansion
risks.rationale: The architecture's interdependence may require coordinated changes across framework and application code when adding more sophisticated options.

non_risks.description: Specialized handlers provide an expansion hook
non_risks.rationale: The existence of application-specific handlers suggests a mechanism for incremental growth.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Extent of specialization supported by handler extensions

scenario_reference.text: Overall consistent behavior expected from the architecture

analysis_records.stimulus: Users observe repeated system behavior across event-processing runs
analysis_records.response_measure: Behavior remains consistent across comparable runs
architectural_decisions: The architecture requires FIFO event dispatch.
There is a single Event Manager and single Event Queue.
The architecture defines component interactions and a base handler hierarchy.
analysis_records.reasoning: A single queue and FIFO dispatch encourage repeatable behavior, and the documented interactions provide a stable execution model. The evidence supports consistency more strongly than most other qualities, although no formal conformance tests are supplied.

non_risks.description: Single FIFO event path supports consistent behavior
non_risks.rationale: One queue and one manager with FIFO dispatch reduce alternative execution paths, making behavior more repeatable.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Strict adherence to FIFO dispatch and single event queue

scenario_reference.text: Hook up multiple applications to the framework at same time

analysis_records.environment: Multiple applications attempt to share the framework
analysis_records.stimulus: More than one application connects to the framework concurrently
analysis_records.response_measure: Applications can use the framework without interference or conflict
architectural_decisions: The architecture exposes only one Event Manager and one Event Queue.
The framework is highly inter-dependent with application logic.
Application-specific handlers exist, but concurrency support is not described.
analysis_records.reasoning: The architecture description does not indicate support for multiple simultaneous applications, and the single manager/queue design suggests a shared point of contention. Without isolation or concurrency mechanisms, safe multi-application use is uncertain.

risks.description: Single shared manager and queue may prevent safe concurrent multi-application use
risks.rationale: Only one Event Manager and one Event Queue are specified, with no isolation or concurrency controls described.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Ability to isolate application-specific event streams

scenario_reference.text: Change interface from command-driven to window-based

analysis_records.stimulus: The system must move from CLI to a window-based interface
analysis_records.response_measure: The interface changes with limited impact on event-processing core
architectural_decisions: The system accepts input via CLI.
Application logic is embedded within framework components.
The Event Manager interacts directly with application handlers.
analysis_records.reasoning: A CLI entry point is explicit, but the event-processing core may or may not be separable from the interface layer because application logic is embedded in framework components. The evidence does not show a clean boundary that would make such a change low cost.

risks.description: Embedded logic may make UI replacement invasive
risks.rationale: If application behavior is embedded in framework components and coupled to CLI input handling, switching to a window-based interface may require broader changes.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Separation between input interface and event-processing core

scenarios.scenario_text: A user enters invalid CLI input while the system is idle, and the framework handles the error without unauthorized access or loss of control.
An event arrives at the CLI, is placed into the single Event Queue, and is dispatched in FIFO order through the Event Manager to the appropriate handler.
A new application-specific handler must be added without changing the existing standard handlers or the event queue contract.
The architecture is adapted from command-driven interaction to a window-based interface while preserving event processing behavior.
Multiple application modules need to share the framework services at the same time without breaking coordinated interaction among components.
